source.title: Same Target, Different Basins: Hard vs. Soft Labels for Annotator Distributions

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports generalization-related outcomes for hard-label versus soft-label training, but it does not test any listed version’s specific claim: it uses annotator-distribution targets rather than arbitrary-label memorization, does not sweep model width or compare convolutional with fully connected architectures or optimizers, and does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates CIFAR-10H held-out performance and training/evaluation loss gaps under different ways of delivering annotator labels. It does not test the mapped versions; results are recorded as findings that fit none of them. Cited results from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study tests annotator-target delivery formats, not V1–V8. Shuffled SLS does not test fitting fixed random labels, and Hessian eigenvalues and traces do not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps. Optimizer, batch size, architecture and regularization are held fixed.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. More precisely, the authors conclude that hard-label delivery is directionally better under simulated sparse annotations, with no individual sparse-sweep comparison surviving Holm correction, and reaches similar endpoints with full distributions. They recommend multipass when raw counts are available and SLS as a lightweight alternative. Hessian geometry and OOD results provide observational or descriptive support.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a CIFAR-adapted ResNet-18 from scratch on CIFAR-10H annotator distributions, comparing soft-label cross-entropy with multipass and stochastic hard-label delivery. It does not use the random-label memorization or generalization-gap protocols in the mapped versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Annotator-count sparsity; whether each example remains paired with its own annotator distribution; how many epochs sampled labels are held fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: All 12 sparse-annotation hard-delivery cells have lower mean soft NLL than soft-label training; nine have unanimous paired-seed improvement. None survives Holm correction. Full-distribution SLS and soft-label endpoints do not differ significantly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On CIFAR-10H with a ResNet-18, hard annotator-target delivery directionally improves posterior quality under simulated sparse annotations and matches soft delivery with full distributions.

fits_no_version.finding: Shuffled SLS reaches soft NLL 2.2973 and approximately 12% hard accuracy when annotator distributions are permuted across inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preserving input-to-annotator-distribution pairing is necessary for effective learning in this delivery-format experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: SLS has lower evaluation-loss Hessian eigenvalue and trace than soft-label training despite similar held-out endpoints. Shuffled SLS has still lower curvature despite near-chance accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Annotator-target delivery changes Hessian curvature, but lower curvature alone does not ensure better held-out performance in this setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 8 plots soft-NLL gap trajectories and reports that SLS reaches its best evaluation epoch about 47.2 epochs earlier, with similar final endpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hard versus soft annotator-target delivery can alter convergence speed while preserving final posterior quality.

record.peer_reviewed: 2nd Workshop on Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning (EIML@ICML 2026)
record.problems: Single dataset and primary architecture; sparse-count conditions are simulated by subsampling a dense annotation pool. The sparse-sweep comparisons use five paired seeds and none survives Holm correction over the 12-cell family. The paper says the OOD family comparisons are descriptive rather than paired hypothesis tests. Geometry analyses are observational. The training/evaluation gap result is figure-only without a textual numeric comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Most Table 2 and Table 3 secondary metrics, Hessian measurements for the high-disagreement slice and the five-seed ablation, OOD detector metrics, additional proper scoring rules, and representation diagnostics were omitted to keep the extraction focused on generalization-related endpoints and curvature; these appear in Tables 2–9 and Figures 8–12. They do not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label memorization alongside natural-label generalization, including held-out chance performance under random labels.
Width increases beyond the threshold for zero training error and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and interventions on local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with training/test error gaps at similarly low training loss, and comparison with norm- and margin-based rankings.
Removal of examples selected by memorization influence versus removal of equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows retain versions ["none"]. Their states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, not judgments that the reported delivery-format effects are absent. These results belong under fits_no_version rather than serving as evidence for the listed claims.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; chance performance on held-out random labels; the listed architectures and settings.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and the specified MNIST/CIFAR-10 settings.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local-connectivity interventions.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and the effects of optimizer tuning, weight decay, or switching optimizers.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions and the specified training-set-size and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness and its ranking of training/test gaps against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
